Paris. The Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen of Sparta triggered the Trojan War, one of antiquity's most destructive conflicts. Originally named Alexandros, he was the son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba. At his birth, a prophecy foretold that he would bring destruction to Troy itself, so his parents exposed him as an infant, leaving him to die in the wilderness. He was found and raised by shepherds in exile on Mount Ida, growing up far from the royal court and the luxuries of the palace. Despite his humble upbringing, his exceptional beauty was eventually recognized, and he was restored to the royal court and his place as a prince of Troy. It was this beauty that led to his most consequential action. Zeus chose him to judge which of three goddesses—Athena, Hera, or Aphrodite—was the most beautiful. Aphrodite bribed him by promising him the love of Helen, the world's most desired woman, so he crowned her the fairest of the three. The Judgment of Paris triggered divine wrath from the scorned goddesses and set in motion all the events leading to the Trojan War. Paris then abducted Helen from her husband Menelaus, king of Sparta, and brought her back to Troy. His action prompted the thousand-ship Greek invasion and the ten-year war that would claim tens of thousands of lives. Yet despite his role in triggering the war, Paris lacked the martial prowess of his brother Hector and the other great Trojan warriors, making him a liability in actual combat. His single genuine moment of warrior achievement came late in the conflict when he killed the invulnerable Achilles with an arrow to his heel, the Greek's only vulnerable point. Later, he was himself killed by Philoctetes' poisoned arrows, a fitting irony for one who had killed with arrows. Paris has long been read as a symbol of the costs of unchecked desire and how individual choices can unleash catastrophic consequences for an entire civilization.
